## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Take the PCP instance c = { (u_1 = "0", v_1 = "11") } over the alphabet {0,1} (a single tile). It has NO solution: any nonempty index sequence i_1...i_m yields concatenations of length m and 2m respectively, and m != 2m, so the two strings can never be equal (exact length count; also confirmed by an exhaustive tile search to depth 10).

Take the one-element structure M for the reduction's signature (constant e, unary function symbols f_0 and f_1, binary relation P):
  domain = {0}
  e^M = 0
  f_0^M(0) = 0, f_1^M(0) = 0   (both letter-functions are the identity)
  P^M = {(0,0)}                (P holds of the unique pair)

Recomputed truth values in M (all quantifiers expanded literally over the 1-element domain):
  phi_1 = P(u_1(e), v_1(e)) = P(0,0) = TRUE
  phi_2 = forall v forall w ( P(v,w) -> P(u_1(v), v_1(w)) ): the only instance is P(0,0) -> P(0,0) = TRUE
  psi   = exists z P(z,z): witness z = 0, since P(0,0) holds = TRUE
So M |= phi_1 /\ phi_2 /\ exists z P(z,z), yet c is not solvable. The witness is convention-independent: it validates phi_1 /\ phi_2 under both word-to-term conventions (letters applied left-to-right and right-to-left), as printed by the script.

A slightly less degenerate witness with a non-total relation on a 2-element domain (also found exhaustively): c = { ("0","00") }, domain {0,1}, e = 0, f_0 = f_1 = constant-0, P = {(0,0)}; again phi_1 /\ phi_2 and exists z P(z,z) hold while c is unsolvable.

Abundance: for c = { ("0","11") }, exhaustive enumeration of ALL 1,119,744 three-element structures found 201,984 models of phi_1 /\ phi_2, of which 192,408 (95.3%) also satisfy exists z P(z,z) — i.e. counterexamples to the "<=" direction are the overwhelming majority of models, not a rare pathology.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The answer claims that whenever a model M satisfies phi_1 and phi_2, the PCP instance c has a solution iff M satisfies "exists z P(z,z)". The backward direction is false: phi_1 and phi_2 only force P to contain the intended pairs (the answer itself notes P may hold "in some other cases as well"), so a model satisfying phi_1 and phi_2 can satisfy "exists z P(z,z)" even when c has no PCP solution. The genuine converse direction of the reduction instead uses one specific term model, not arbitrary models satisfying phi_1 and phi_2.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> If $P(v,w)$ indeed has that meaning (which is what happens if $\mathcal{M}$ satisfies $\varphi_1\land\varphi_2$), then $c\in\mathcal{C}\iff \exists z P(z,z)$.

Context of the original problem:

> What is the purpose of interpreting elements in the proof of reduction of PCP to validity decidability problem of predicate logic?
> 
> Since my question relates directly to a part of the text from a 2004 book, *Logic in Computer Science: Modelling and Reasoning about Systems (2nd Edition) by Michael Huth and Mark Ryan*, in order to provide context for the following discussion, I'm partially quoting the book verbatim:
> 
> > The decision problem of validity in predicate logic is undecidable: no program exists which, given any $\varphi$, decides whether $\varphi$.
> 
> > PROOF: As said before, we pretend that validity is decidable for predicate logic and thereby solve the (insoluble) Post correspondence problem. Given a correspondence problem instance $C$:
> $$s_1 s_2 ... s_k$$ $$t_1 t_2 ... t_k$$
> we need to be able to construct, within finite space and time and uniformly so for all instances, some for [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The sentence asserts that satisfying phi_1 /\ phi_2 already pins P down to "its intended meaning", and hence that for any such model M, c in C  <=>  M |= exists z P(z,z). Formalizing the reduction in the standard way — phi_1 := /\_i P(u_i(e), v_i(e)) and phi_2 := forall v forall w (P(v,w) -> /\_i P(u_i(v), v_i(w))) — both formulas are purely positive Horn-style closure conditions: they only ever FORCE pairs INTO P and contain no minimality, freeness or induction axiom. Consequently any structure in which P is (a superset of) the intended relation is still a model, and in particular the trivial structure that collapses everything to one point and makes P total is a model of phi_1 /\ phi_2 for every PCP instance whatsoever. That structure satisfies exists z P(z,z) unconditionally, so the "<=" direction ("M |= exists z P(z,z) implies c has a solution") fails outright.

The exhaustive search confirms this mechanically: over 1332 small PCP instances and all structures of size <= 2, every one of the 144 instances that are certified unsolvable (by the exact length certificate |u_i| < |v_i| for all i, or |u_i| > |v_i| for all i) admits a model of phi_1 /\ phi_2 that also satisfies exists z P(z,z) — 44,224 (instance, structure, convention) counterexample triples in total. The claim's "=>" direction (a solution forces P(z,z) in every model) is the sound half; only the converse breaks. The correct statement is that phi_1 /\ phi_2 -> exists z P(z,z) is VALID iff c has a solution, and the converse half of that is proved by exhibiting ONE specific model — the free/term model over e, f_0, f_1 with P interpreted as the least relation closed under the tile rules — in which P really does hold only of intended pairs. Quantifying over arbitrary models, as the sentence does, is what makes it false.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

The only inference that can license the quoted "therefore" is the schema (S): "L is not regular => h(L) is not regular" for a homomorphism h. An exhaustive scan of 156 (language, homomorphism) pairs — 6 catalogue languages with decidable membership crossed with ALL non-erasing homomorphisms h: Sigma* -> {c,d}* with |h(x)| in {1,2} — found 22 pairs refuting (S). Flagship witness: L = {a^n b^n : n >= 1}, h(a) = h(b) = c (non-erasing, so the counterexample is not an artefact of erasing letters). Then h(L) = {c^(2n) : n >= 1}, which the script certifies regular by constructing a 4-state DFA (q0 start; q0 -c-> q1, q1 -c-> q3 accepting, q3 -c-> q1, any d -> dead q2) and simulating it against the exactly computed truth table of "v in h(L)" on ALL 8191 strings of {c,d}^<=12 with perfect agreement. The image table is exact because |h(w)| >= |w| for non-erasing h, so every image word of length <= 12 has a preimage of length <= 12 (finite enumeration). L's non-regularity is certified mechanically as a Myhill–Nerode lower bound: 15 pairwise inequivalent restricted residuals (prefixes and suffixes up to length 7), i.e. no DFA with fewer than 15 states recognises L; that its Nerode index is actually infinite is the standard textbook theorem. Other refuting pairs include palindromes with h(a)=h(b)=c (image = c^+, 3 states) and {a^n b^m : n>m} with h(a)=h(b)=c. Additionally, on the proof's OWN language the script gives an exact closed-form instance: P = {0^p : p prime} with g(0) = epsilon yields g(P) = {epsilon} exactly (verified over all primes <= 200, and trivially for all p), a one-word hence regular language, while P is not regular.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **Example 2 relies on the inference schema "L is irregular, therefore its homomorphic image h(L) is irregular" (applied to P = {0^p : p prime}). This forward direction is invalid: regular languages are closed under homomorphism, so only the contrapositive direction (h(L) irregular implies L irregular, as used in Example 1) is sound; irregularity is not preserved under homomorphisms in general. (Additionally, h is defined backwards: h: {0} -> {1} with rule h(1)=0.)**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Defined $h: \{0\} \to \{1\}$ as $h(1)=0$.
> It follows that $h(P) =  $\{1^p : p \text{ is a primes}\}$ and therefore is irregular.

Context of the original problem:

> How to use homomorphisms to prove irregularity

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The proof step writes "h(P) = {1^p : p prime} and therefore is irregular", where the only support for "therefore" is that P was already known irregular — i.e. the forward schema (S). Regular languages are closed under homomorphism, which yields only the contrapositive (h(L) irregular => L irregular, the sound direction used in Example 1); (S) itself is unsound. The witness makes this concrete: L = {a^n b^n : n>=1} is not regular (mechanically certified: >= 15 Nerode classes, so no DFA with <= 14 states; classically infinitely many), yet under the non-erasing homomorphism h(a)=h(b)=c the image h(L) = {c^(2n) : n>=1} IS regular, verified by an explicit 4-state DFA that agrees with h(L) on every one of the 8191 strings of {c,d}^<=12. Schema (S) predicts "h(L) not regular"; here h(L) is regular, so (S) is false and the "therefore" is unlicensed. Honest scope note: the flagged conclusion of Example 2 happens to be TRUE — the negative control shows all 12 non-erasing unary homomorphisms leave {a^p : p prime} without a small DFA, and indeed {1^p : p prime} is genuinely irregular; what is refuted is the inference used, not the end result. The secondary textual defect is confirmed by inspection with no search needed: the sentence declares h: {0} -> {1} but then defines h(1)=0, defining h on a letter outside the stated domain alphabet, whereas the subsequent use h(P) = {1^p} requires h(0)=1 — the definition is written backwards relative to its use.

Take n=6, A={1,1,1,1,1,1}, and t=2. All a_i and t are positive integers. Then P(x)=(1+x)^6, so c_2=C(6,2)=15, while nt=6·2=12. Thus c_2>nt, even at j=t.

The flagged claim: **Every coefficient of A(x)=∏ᵢ(1+x^{aᵢ}) is at most nt.**

> Note that this polynomial is $\Pi$-$O(n)$-sparse, and that when expanded, each coefficient in the polynomial is bounded from above by $nt$.

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

The coefficient c_2 counts two-element selections among six distinct occurrences of 1. There are exactly 15 such subsets, contradicting the asserted upper bound 12.

## Object

The `mst` family of the Part-B bug bank: a reference implementation with
seeded, realistic (LLM-slip-style) mutants, ported bit-exactly to Lean 4 as the
trusted library `QEDBugBank` (plain `Nat`/`List` data, structural recursion
only, so the kernel itself evaluates every run).

- Reference: `kruskalMST` — Kruskal with union-by-rank, a Lean port bit-exact to the Python reference.
- Observable: `mstObsEq`: total weight **and** the chosen-edge list in acceptance order.
- Seeded mutants admitted by the Python bank:
- `mutant_2_equal_rank_skip` — union-by-rank silently skips the merge when ranks are equal
- `mutant_3_early_stop` — off-by-one termination: stops after n-2 accepted edges
- `mutant_4_stale_group_union` — equal-weight edge groups judged against a stale component snapshot
- Enumerated witness space: all 3,834 connected weighted graphs with exactly n = 4 vertices, weights in {1,2,3} (`allMstGraphs 4`).

## What it kills

The illusion that these mutants are benign — i.e. the claim that no small input
distinguishes them from the reference. Each admitted (mutant, test) pair
carries a kernel-checked admission theorem
`adm_mst__<mutant>__<test>` on its minimal canonical killing input:

- `mutant_2_equal_rank_skip` killed by `test_differential_float_weights_total`
- `mutant_2_equal_rank_skip` killed by `test_differential_int_weights_total`

The admission combinator proves, on the witness `w`: the reference satisfies

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

n = 1 is an explicit witness, and every n in 1..10 is also a witness.

(a) The stated base case is arithmetically false. G_1 has no edges, so R(1) = 0 (confirmed by simulation under all three Dijkstra variants). But 2^1 - 1 = 1. The proof writes "R(1) = 0 = 2^1 - 1", i.e. 0 = 1. Hence the claim R(n) >= 2^n - 1 already fails at its own base case: claim says R(1) >= 1; here R(1) = 0 < 1.

(b) The inductive closing step "2^n - 2 >= 2^n - 1" is false for every n (checked exactly for n = 1..2000): LHS - RHS = -1 always; e.g. n = 1 gives 0 >= 1.

(c) The actual Relax counts on G_n are polynomial, not exponential, so the claim fails for every n tested, under every tie-breaking of the priority queue. Exhaustive maximum-over-all-executions results (n : variant A = CLRS no-reinsertion / variant B = lazy PQ with re-insertion, stale pops skipped / variant C = lazy PQ with re-insertion, stale pops relax / 2^n - 1):
  n=1: 0 / 0 / 0 vs 1
  n=2: 1 / 1 / 1 vs 3
  n=3: 3 / 3 / 3 vs 7
  n=4: 6 / 7 / 7 vs 15
  n=5: 10 / 14 / 14 vs 31
  n=6: 15 / 25 / 25 vs 63
  n=7: 21 / 41 / 41 vs 127
  n=8: 28 / 63 / 63 vs 255
  n=9: 36 / 92 / 92 vs 511
  n=10: 45 / 129 / 129 vs 1023
For example at n = 10: the claim says R(10) >= 2^10 - 1 = 1023; the maximum over ALL executions is R(10) = 129 < 1023 (and only 45 for textbook Dijkstra). The re-insertion counts 0,1,3,7,14,25,41,63,92,129 have constant third differences (second differences 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8), i.e. they grow like a cubic in n, not like 2^n. For textbook Dijkstra R(n) = |E_n| = n(n-1)/2, and n(n-1)/2 >= 2^n - 1 was verified to fail for all 200 values n = 1..200 (it holds for NONE of them).

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The proof's central quantitative claim, established "by induction", that the number R(n) of Relax invocations performed by Dijkstra on the constructed complete-DAG family G_n (V_n = {v_0,...,v_{n-1}}, E_n = all (v_i,v_j) with i<j, w(v_i,v_j) = -2^i) satisfies R(n) >= 2^n - 1, together with its stated base case R(1) = 0 = 2^1 - 1 and its inductive closing step "2^n - 2 >= 2^n - 1".**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Base case (n = 1): G1 has no edges, R(1) = 0 = 21 −1

Context of the original problem:

> Problem Statement
> Problem: Algorithms - 21
> Prove that the inclusion of negative edge weights forces Dijkstra’s algorithm to execute
> Ω(2V ) relaxation steps in the worst-case scenario, irrespective of whether the graph is
> acyclic. To substantiate this, explicitly define a family of weighted directed acyclic graphs
> (DAGs), denoted Gn, where each graph contains n vertices for any given positive integer
> n. Prove that processing Gn with Dijkstra’s algorithm necessitates Ω(2n) invocations of
> the Relax operation.
> 1

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The asserted statement is: for the specific finite graph family G_n (V_n = {v_0..v_{n-1}}, E_n = all (v_i,v_j) with i<j, w(v_i,v_j) = -2^i), Dijkstra from v_0 performs R(n) >= 2^n - 1 Relax invocations, proved by induction with base case R(1) = 0 = 2^1 - 1 and closing step 2^n - 2 >= 2^n - 1. For each fixed n this is a finite, decidable statement (finite graph, finite algorithm run), so it is finitely refutable.

Three independent refutations were computed with exact integer arithmetic:

1. Base-case arithmetic. 2^1 - 1 = 1, not 0. The proof's own base case asserts 0 = 1. Since G_1 has a single vertex and no edges, R(1) = 0 under any implementation, so R(1) >= 2^1 - 1 is FALSE at n = 1. The induction therefore has no valid base.

2. Closing-step arithmetic. "2^n - 2 >= 2^n - 1" is equivalent to -2 >= -1, false for every n; verified exactly for n = 1..2000. So even granting the inductive hypothesis, the step from 2(2^{n-1} - 1) = 2^n - 2 to the required 2^n - 1 is an unjustified strengthening in the wrong direction.

3. The quantitative claim itself is false, not merely mis-proved. I simulated Dijkstra on G_n and counted Relax invocations for three standard variants: (A) CLRS Dijkstra where each vertex is Extract-Min'ed once and its out-edges relaxed once; (B) a lazy priority queue that re-inserts a vertex whenever its tentative distance strictly decreases, skipping stale pops; (C) the same lazy queue but relaxing on every pop including stale ones. For B and C I did an exhaustive memoized DFS over EVERY minimum-key tie-breaking the queue could make, so the reported value is the maximum over all possible executions of that variant; this was completed for n = 1..10 (n = 11,12 exceeded the 400k-state cap and are reported n/a, not claimed). In all cases R_max(n) < 2^n - 1 for every n <= 10, so no implementation choice and no tie-break rule can rescue the bound on these instances. The structural reason is visible in the construction: every out-edge of v_i has the SAME weight -2^i regardless of the head, so once v_i is popped with its final label, all of its out-edges are relaxed with identical decrements and no cascading re-relaxation chain of exponential length is created; the counts grow cubically. For the textbook variant, R(n) = |E_n| = n(n-1)/2, and n(n-1)/2 >= 2^n - 1 holds for none of n = 1..200.

Confidence is high: the n = 1 refutation is variant-independent and requires no modelling assumptions (a graph with no edges admits zero Relax calls, while 2^1 - 1 = 1), and the arithmetic falsehood of "2^n - 2 >= 2^n - 1" is unconditional. The broader n <= 10 refutation depends on modelling choices for what "Dijkstra" and "Relax invocation" mean, which is why three variants were covered, each maximized over all tie-breakings.

## Object

The certificate witness, as recorded by the triage stage:

Use G=K2 with vertices {1,2}, edge (1,2), and ferry capacity k=2, so Charon can carry at most k−1=1 passenger. G has a vertex cover of size 1, e.g. {1}. But with exactly one crossing under the original transport goal, at most one passenger can be moved, leaving the other on the starting bank; hence no one-crossing valid solution reaches the final state. A checker can enumerate the possible one-crossing passenger sets of size ≤1 and verify none equals V.

## What it kills

The flawed step of QEDBench problem Algorithms_11, solution 2, reads:

> If we restrict the number of crossings to exactly 1 (one-way trip), the problem is exactly: ”Does there exist a vertex cover of size ≤k −1?”.

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its
conclusion, refuting the step **as written** (not necessarily the problem's
headline theorem — see the module docstring for scope).

## Why it works

From the Lean module docstring
(`lean/qedbench/ProofCerts/Algorithms/Alg11.lean`):

**Algorithms_11 (sol1/2) — the VC ↔ river-crossing reduction equivalence fails**

Both candidate solutions reduce Vertex Cover to an Alcuin-style river-crossing puzzle:
the items to ferry are the vertices of a conflict graph `G`; the boat holds the ferryman
(Charon) plus at most `k − 1` items per crossing; a state is *safe* when the bank
**without** Charon contains no edge of `G` with both endpoints present; initially Charon
and all items are on the left bank, and the goal is everyone on the right bank. The
solutions assert the equivalences:

* **sol1**: "`G` has a vertex cover of size `≤ K` **iff** the river-crossing instance
  `(G, k = K + 1)` is feasible."
* **sol2**: "with exactly **one** crossing the instance is solvable **iff** `G` has a
  vertex cover of size `≤ k − 1`."

Both are **false** in the direction "vertex cover exists ⇒ the crossing succeeds".

**Counterexample to sol1 (`K = 1`, `G = K₁,₃`).** The star `K₁,₃` with center `c` and
leaves `x, y, z` (edges `c–x`, `c–y`, `c–z`) has the vertex cover `{c}` of size
`1 ≤ K = 1` (`vcC_covers`, `vcC_size_one`). The claimed equivalent crossing instance has
`k = K + 1 = 2`: Charon plus at most **one** item per crossing. That instance is
**infeasible** (the ferrying number of `K₁,₃` is `2`, not `1`): from the start Charon can
only ferry `c` (anything else strands `c` with a leaf), after which every continuation
shuttles among the nine states
`{0, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 16, 19}` — Charon can park `c` on the right, fetch one leaf, and
then must take `c` back before fetching the next leaf, undoing all progress. The
all-on-the-right state `31` is never reached. We certify unreachability in the `GT1`
closure-invariant style: the explicit `9`-state set `inReach` (given by the bitmask
`reachMask = 592285`) contains the start state (`start_in_reach`), is **closed** under
every legal-and-safe move (`reach_closed`), and excludes the goal (`goal_not_in_reach`).
Any feasible crossing schedule visits a `step`-path of states from `startState` to
`goalState`; a start-containing `step`-closed set traps every such path, so the goal
being outside `inReach` means **no schedule exists**. For emphasis, `safe_goal` shows
the goal state itself is safe (infeasibility is genuinely a reachability obstruction),
and `start_moves` shows ferrying `c` is the *only* legal first move.

**Counterexample to sol2 (`G = K₂`, `k = 2`).** `K₂` (vertices `v₀, v₁`, one edge) has
the vertex cover `{v₁}` of size `1 = k − 1` (`vcH_covers`, `vcH_size_one`). But ONE
crossing moves Charon plus at most `k − 1 = 1` item, so at least one of the two items
stays on the left bank: enumerating all `8` candidate post-crossing states, the legal
outcomes from the start are exactly `{1, 3, 5}` (carry nothing / carry `v₀` / carry
`v₁`) — never the goal state `7` (`one_crossing_outcomes`, `one_crossing_capacity`).
So "solvable with exactly one crossing" fails although a vertex cover of size `k − 1`
exists, refuting sol2's equivalence (its "if" direction).

**Modeling choices**

* **sol1 state space**: a state is `Fin 32`, read as five bits — bit `0` is Charon's
  side, bit `i + 1` is the side of item `i` (`0 = c`, `1 = x`, `2 = y`, `3 = z`);
  side `false`/`0` = left (start) bank, `true`/`1` = right (goal) bank. So
  `startState = 0` and `goalState = 31`. Bits are extracted with the kernel-accelerated
  operations `>>>`, `%`, `==` only.
* `edgesG` lists the three star edges; `safe s` says no edge has both endpoints on the
  Charon-less bank. A move `legalMove p s` requires: Charon switches banks; at most one
  item changes banks (`movedCount p s ≤ 1` via `Nat.ble`, i.e. boat capacity
  `k = 2` counting Charon); and any item that moves starts on Charon's old bank
  (`ridesWithCharon` — it rides the boat, hence lands on Charon's new bank).
  `step p s = legalMove p s && safe s` demands safety only of the **target** state;
  this is *more permissive* than the real puzzle (which also needs `safe p`), so our
  unreachability certificate is only **stronger**.
* `inReach` is membership in the bitmask `reachMask = 592285`, whose set bits
  `{0, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 16, 19}` are exactly the BFS closure of the start state under
  `step` (verified numerically). All facts are `decide`-checked over `Fin 32` pairs —
  no `Finset`, no function-type enumeration, no `native_decide`, in the style of `GT1`'s
  separator certificate (`A_closed`).
* **sol2 state space**: `Fin 8` (bit `0` Charon, bits `1`–`2` the two `K₂` vertices),
  `startH = 0`, `goalH = 7`, same move rules with capacity `k − 1 = 1`. The claim's
  "solvable with exactly one crossing" is the decidable proposition `Sol2Claim`:
  some state reachable in one legal safe crossing equals `goalH`; it is refuted in the
  `GT20` unpacking style (`sol2_claim_fails`).
* Vertex covers are `Bool`-valued membership functions; `coversG`/`coversH` check every
  listed edge has a covered endpoint, and sizes are explicit sums of `Bool.toNat`
  (no `Finset.card`), as in `GT1`'s `degree`.

- The witness is a minimal, machine-checked regression input for any proof or
  implementation that leans on this step; rebuilding the Lean module re-verifies it.
- The module states the claim faithfully in Mathlib vocabulary; its definitions
  can be reused to audit neighboring steps of the same proof.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Minimal witness (m = 2 bits, n = 2 strings), found by exhaustive enumeration and reproduced by the script.

Setting: LSD radix sort with stable counting-sort passes; bit positions indexed 1..m from most significant (left) to least significant (right); passes run pos = m, m-1, ..., 1, so "later passes" use MORE significant positions k < j.

Input array (in order): ["01", "10"].
Take j = 2 (the last/least-significant position, whose pass the sentence appeals to).

Pass keyed on bit j = 2 (stable): "01" has bit2 = 1, "10" has bit2 = 0, so the array becomes A = ["10", "01"]. The position-j groups are G_0 = {"10"} and G_1 = {"01"}, and in A every member of G_0 precedes every member of G_1.

Later pass, keyed on bit k = 1 (k < j, more significant): "01" has bit1 = 0, "10" has bit1 = 1, so the stable pass yields B = ["01", "10"].

Formal violation of the quoted sentence: a permutation that "only reorders strings within the groups that share the same bit at position j" can never change the relative order of two strings lying in different groups. Here u = "10" (bit_j = 0) and v = "01" (bit_j = 1) lie in different position-j groups, and
  index_A(u) = 0 < index_A(v) = 1  (u before v),
  index_B(u) = 1 > index_B(v) = 0  (u after v).
Claim says index_B(u) < index_B(v); here index_B(u) = 1 > index_B(v) = 0. The later pass moved a string from one position-j group ahead of a string from the other group, i.e. it interleaved the groups rather than reordering within them.

This is not an isolated accident: the exhaustive scan found the violation in 1,100,924 of the 1,157,264 arrays searched (e.g. 2 of the 16 arrays already at m = n = 2).

Secondary exhaustive check over the same 1,157,264 arrays: the proof's CONCLUSION (if s_i = t_i for all i < j, s_j = 0, t_j = 1, then s never ends up after t in the final array) has NO counterexample. So the theorem stands; it is exactly the quoted justification that is false, and it is false for the reason stated in the target claim — the correct argument needs the unused hypothesis s_i = t_i for all i < j (which makes s and t have equal keys in every later pass, so plain stability preserves their order), not any "later passes only permute within position-j groups" property.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The proof's stated justification for the crucial stability step: that the passes after iteration k=j "only reorder strings within the groups that share the same bit at position j". This universal claim about later stable counting-sort passes is false; a stable sort by a more significant bit k<j freely interleaves strings drawn from the two position-j groups. The proof's conclusion (s cannot move ahead of t) actually requires the unused hypothesis s_i = t_i for all i<j, which this sentence never invokes.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> those later sorts are *stable* and only reorder strings **within** the groups that share the same bit at position j

Context of the original problem:

> Problem Statement
> Problem: Algorithms - 30
> Consider a collection of n binary strings, where each string has length m. The lexico-
> graphical order is defined as follows: for strings s and t, we define s < t if there is a
> position j ∈{1, . . . , m} such that sj < tj and si = ti for all indices 1 ≤i < j. Prove
> the existence of an algorithm that sorts these n strings according to this lexicographical
> order with a total running time of O(nm).
> 1

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The sentence asserts a universal property of every later stable counting-sort pass: that such a pass only reorders strings within the blocks determined by the bit at position j. A permutation that acts only within blocks is exactly one that preserves the relative order of any two elements in different blocks, so the assertion is a finitely-quantified statement over finite arrays of finite binary strings and is refuted by a single array + j + k + pair whose relative order flips. The script enumerates every array in ({0,1}^m)^n for m in {2,3,4,5}, n in {2,3,4} (1,157,264 arrays, repetitions allowed, entries tracked by identity index so duplicates are handled), runs the full LSD radix sort, snapshots the array after each pass, and tests the block-order-preservation condition for every j, every later key position k < j, and every pair of entries. All computation is exact and combinatorial (ints, tuples of 0/1 bits, index comparisons); no floats, no randomness, deterministic itertools.product enumeration. A violation was found immediately at m = n = 2 with input ["01","10"], j = 2, k = 1, and in 95.1% of all arrays searched. A second exhaustive pass over the same space confirmed zero violations of the statement the proof was actually trying to prove, isolating the defect to the justification (which never invokes the hypothesis s_i = t_i for i < j) rather than to the theorem.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Work in ℤ. Let a=2, b=4, and S={2u+4v | u,v∈ℤ, 2u+4v≠0}. Take ν(n)=|n|. Designate g=2 as gcd{a,b}. Choose u=-1, v=0, so d=2(-1)+4(0)=-2∈S. Every element of S is a nonzero even integer, hence has ν≥2, while ν(d)=2; thus d has minimal valuation.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The proof claims that the chosen minimal-valuation linear combination d equals the designated gcd as an element, although the preceding divisibility and valuation facts establish at most that they are associates.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Since $d$ is the element of $S$ such that $\map \nu d$ is the smallest element of $\nu \sqbrk S$:
> $\gcd \set {a, b} = d = u \times a + v \times b$

Context of the original problem:

> Title: Bézout's Identity/Euclidean Domain
> 
> Let $\struct {D, +, \times}$ be a Euclidean domain whose zero is $0$ and whose unity is $1$.
> 
> Let $\nu: D \setminus \set 0 \to \N$ be the Euclidean valuation on $D$.
> 
> Let $a, b \in D$ such that $a$ and $b$ are not both equal to $0$.
> 
> Let $\gcd \set {a, b}$ be the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$.
> 
> [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

The claimed element equality is g=d, i.e. 2=-2, which is false. The established conclusion is only association: d=(-1)g, and -1 is a unit. Both divide a and b, and every common divisor of a and b divides both g and d.

> verify.py ran successfully and deterministically. The witness satisfies the stated integer hypotheses but refutes literal equality of the designated gcd and the chosen minimal-valuation combination.

> Actual result: 2=-2 is false

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Minimal witness (m = 2 bits, n = 2 strings), found by exhaustive enumeration and reproduced by the script.

Setting: LSD radix sort with stable counting-sort passes; bit positions indexed 1..m from most significant (left) to least significant (right); passes run pos = m, m-1, ..., 1, so "later passes" use MORE significant positions k < j.

Input array (in order): ["01", "10"].
Take j = 2 (the last/least-significant position, whose pass the sentence appeals to).

Pass keyed on bit j = 2 (stable): "01" has bit2 = 1, "10" has bit2 = 0, so the array becomes A = ["10", "01"]. The position-j groups are G_0 = {"10"} and G_1 = {"01"}, and in A every member of G_0 precedes every member of G_1.

Later pass, keyed on bit k = 1 (k < j, more significant): "01" has bit1 = 0, "10" has bit1 = 1, so the stable pass yields B = ["01", "10"].

Formal violation of the quoted sentence: a permutation that "only reorders strings within the groups that share the same bit at position j" can never change the relative order of two strings lying in different groups. Here u = "10" (bit_j = 0) and v = "01" (bit_j = 1) lie in different position-j groups, and
  index_A(u) = 0 < index_A(v) = 1  (u before v),
  index_B(u) = 1 > index_B(v) = 0  (u after v).
Claim says index_B(u) < index_B(v); here index_B(u) = 1 > index_B(v) = 0. The later pass moved a string from one position-j group ahead of a string from the other group, i.e. it interleaved the groups rather than reordering within them.

This is not an isolated accident: the exhaustive scan found the violation in 1,100,924 of the 1,157,264 arrays searched (e.g. 2 of the 16 arrays already at m = n = 2).

Secondary exhaustive check over the same 1,157,264 arrays: the proof's CONCLUSION (if s_i = t_i for all i < j, s_j = 0, t_j = 1, then s never ends up after t in the final array) has NO counterexample. So the theorem stands; it is exactly the quoted justification that is false, and it is false for the reason stated in the target claim — the correct argument needs the unused hypothesis s_i = t_i for all i < j (which makes s and t have equal keys in every later pass, so plain stability preserves their order), not any "later passes only permute within position-j groups" property.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The proof's stated justification for the crucial stability step: that the passes after iteration k=j "only reorder strings within the groups that share the same bit at position j". This universal claim about later stable counting-sort passes is false; a stable sort by a more significant bit k<j freely interleaves strings drawn from the two position-j groups. The proof's conclusion (s cannot move ahead of t) actually requires the unused hypothesis s_i = t_i for all i<j, which this sentence never invokes.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> those later sorts are *stable* and only reorder strings **within** the groups that share the same bit at position j

Context of the original problem:

> Problem Statement
> Problem: Algorithms - 30
> Consider a collection of n binary strings, where each string has length m. The lexico-
> graphical order is defined as follows: for strings s and t, we define s < t if there is a
> position j ∈{1, . . . , m} such that sj < tj and si = ti for all indices 1 ≤i < j. Prove
> the existence of an algorithm that sorts these n strings according to this lexicographical
> order with a total running time of O(nm).
> 1

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

The sentence asserts a universal property of every later stable counting-sort pass: that such a pass only reorders strings within the blocks determined by the bit at position j. A permutation that acts only within blocks is exactly one that preserves the relative order of any two elements in different blocks, so the assertion is a finitely-quantified statement over finite arrays of finite binary strings and is refuted by a single array + j + k + pair whose relative order flips. A violation was found immediately at m = n = 2 with input ["01","10"], j = 2, k = 1, and in 95.1% of all arrays searched. A second exhaustive pass over the same space confirmed zero violations of the statement the proof was actually trying to prove, isolating the defect to the justification (which never invokes the hypothesis s_i = t_i for i < j) rather than to the theorem.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Take the length-2 integer array A = [2, 3], i.e. A[0] = 2 and A[1] = 3, which satisfies the stated precondition exactly. Execute the single assignment A[A[0]-1] := A[0]. The index expression evaluates to A[0]-1 = 2-1 = 1 and the right-hand side to A[0] = 2, so the statement is the write A[1] := 2. The post-state is A = [2, 2], i.e. A[0] = 2 and A[1] = 2. The claimed "correct postcondition" A[0] = 1 AND A[1] = 1 is false on both conjuncts: A[0] = 2 != 1 and A[1] = 2 != 1. The same holds for any longer array with A[0]=2, A[1]=3 (e.g. A = [2,3,0] -> [2,2,0]); the trailing cells are irrelevant. Reproduce by hand in three arithmetic steps, or by running the script (runtime 0.05 s).

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The answer claims that executing the assignment A[A[0]-1] := A[0] from a state satisfying the precondition A[0] = 2 AND A[1] = 3 yields the "correct postcondition" A[0] = 1 AND A[1] = 1.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> consider the assignment $A[A[0]-1] := A[0]$ under the precondition $A[0] = 2 \wedge A[1] = 3$: you cannot make a simple substitution to obtain the correct postcondition $A[0] = 1 \wedge A[1] = 1$

Context of the original problem:

> How to deal with arrays during Hoare-style correctness proofs
> 
> In the discussion around [this question](https://cs.stackexchange.com/q/1157/98), Gilles mentions correctly that any correctness proof of an algorithm that uses arrays has to prove that there are no out-of-bounds array accesses; depending on the runtime model, this would cause a runtime error or access to non-array elements.
> 
> One common technique to perform such correctness proofs (at least in undergrad studies and probably in automated verification) is by using [Hoare logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoare_logic). I am not aware that the standard set of rules containes anything relating to arrays; they seem to be restricted to monadic variables.
> 
> I can imagine adding axioms of the form
> 
> $\qquad \displaystyle \frac{}{\{0 \leq i \lt A.\mathrm{length} \land {P[A[i]/E]} \}\ A[i] := E;\ \{P\}}$
> 
> [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The statement A[A[0]-1] := A[0] writes to exactly one cell, index A[0]-1. Under the precondition A[0] = 2 that index is 1, so the only cell modified is A[1], and it receives the value A[0] = 2. Consequently (i) A[0] is not written at all, so A[0] = 2 in every post-state, immediately falsifying the conjunct A[0] = 1; and (ii) A[1] becomes 2, falsifying A[1] = 1. The strongest postcondition of this assignment under the given precondition is A[0] = 2 AND A[1] = 2, not A[0] = 1 AND A[1] = 1. The exhaustive run confirms 0 out of 7140 (in-precondition state, semantics-reading) pairs satisfy the asserted postcondition — the failure rate is 100%, so the example as written in the proof is simply arithmetically wrong, not merely a case where "simple substitution" is inadequate. The refutation is robust to semantic quibbles: three operational readings were modelled (index and RHS both evaluated in the pre-state; an aliasing/sequential reading where the RHS is re-read after the write; and an RHS-first reading) and all yield A = [2,2]. It is also robust to the indexing convention: even if one insisted on 1-based arrays with A[0] a legal slot, the write is still A[1] := 2, giving A[1] = 2 != 1. (Note that under a genuinely 1-based convention A[0] would not exist at all, so the precondition itself would be ill-formed.) A plausible intended example would have been something like A[A[0]-1] := A[0]-1 or different constants; as printed, the asserted postcondition is unreachable from the asserted precondition.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Non-degenerate witness (genuine gap m >= 2), smallest of its kind found by exhaustive enumeration:

  N = 5, m = 2, A = (x_0,...,x_4) = [3, 4, 2, 5, 1]

  Gap-m chain through position 0: x_0, x_2, x_4 = 3, 2, 1.
  Hypothesis of the claim holds: at the first insertion step (i = m = 2) we compare x_2 = 2 with x_0 = 3; since 2 < 3 they exchange places, i.e. "x_0 switches place with x_m during the first pass".
  After the full m-sort (gap-2 insertion sort, equivalently sorting each residue chain in place):

  B = m-sort(A) = [1, 4, 2, 5, 3]

  The claim says B[0] == x_m = 2; here B[0] = 1 != 2. In fact B[0] = 1 = x_4 = x_{2m}, the minimum of the whole gap-m chain {x_0, x_m, x_{2m}} = {3, 2, 1} — exactly the failure mode described in the target claim.

Smallest witness overall (degenerate gap m = 1, i.e. plain insertion sort): N = 3, A = [3, 2, 1]; x_1 = 2 < 3 = x_0 so they swap on the first step, but B = [1, 2, 3] and B[0] = 1 = x_2 != x_1 = 2.

The script also verified, over all 36243 counterexamples found, that B[0] always equals min{x_0, x_m, x_{2m}, ...} (0 exceptions), confirming the stated diagnosis rather than merely the negation.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The proof asserts that if x_0 switches place with x_m during the first pass of m-sorting, then the final m-sorted array B starts with the entry x_m regardless of where x_0 moves afterwards. This is used to conclude the chain x_m < x_0 < x_n < x_k and hence that B is n-sorted. In fact B's first entry is the minimum of the entire gap-m subsequence through position 0, which can be x_{2m} (or a later element), not x_m.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Say that after first pass $x_0$ switches place with $x_m$, so the final array $B$ starts with the entry $x_m$ regardless of the position of $x_0$ (which can further switch place with $x_{2m}$ and so on). Thus, $x_m < x_0$.

Context of the original problem:

> Proof: "If the list is then k-sorted for some smaller integer k, then the list remains h-sorted"

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The asserted implication is: if during the first insertion step of m-sorting x_0 and x_m exchange places (equivalently x_m < x_0), then the final m-sorted array B satisfies B[0] = x_m.

This is false. m-sorting sorts each gap-m residue chain, so B[0] = min{x_0, x_m, x_{2m}, x_{3m}, ...} — the minimum over the entire chain through position 0, not merely the smaller of x_0 and x_m. Whenever some later chain element is smaller than x_m, the element x_m is itself displaced further right by a subsequent insertion, and it is that later element that ends up in position 0. The parenthetical in the proof ("which can further switch place with x_{2m} and so on") tracks x_0 moving right but overlooks that x_m moves right in exactly the same way.

Consequence for the proof: the identification of B's first entry with x_m is unjustified, so the chain of inequalities x_m < x_0 < x_n < x_k that is derived from "B starts with x_m" is not supported by this argument. (The weaker fact x_m < x_0 does follow directly from the swap hypothesis, but the step that names B[0] as x_m — and hence the link into the rest of the chain — fails.)

## Object

Classical constructions iterate a self-similar rearrangement of the square (Peano
1890, Hilbert 1891): a uniformly convergent sequence of piecewise-linear curves whose
limit hits every point. A slicker route (reflected in mathlib's proof): map the Cantor
set continuously onto [0,1]² via interleaved binary digits, then extend to [0,1] by
linear interpolation across the removed intervals.

## What it kills

The pre-1890 notion that "curve = 1-dimensional object." Cardinality already showed
|[0,1]| = |[0,1]²| (Cantor), but continuity was believed to forbid it; Peano showed
only *injectivity+continuity* forbids it.

## Debugging uses

- Any proof estimating the "size" of a continuous image by the dimension of the domain
  (Hausdorff dimension, measure, covering numbers) needs Lipschitz or Hölder control:
  a merely continuous image of a null set can have positive area. Lipschitz maps do
  not increase Hausdorff dimension — continuity alone does nothing.
- Space-filling curves are also a *tool*: Hilbert-curve indexing linearizes 2D data
  while roughly preserving locality (databases, load balancing). The counterexample
  and the data structure are the same object; the pathology is the feature.
- Parametrization traps: "parametrize the boundary/region by arc length" assumes
  rectifiability. Space-filling curves have infinite length on every subinterval —
  the extreme case of the Schwarz-lantern lesson that length/area interact badly
  with limits.

## References

Mathlib: `exists_peano_curve` (Counterexamples library). Classical: Peano (1890),
Hilbert (1891); Hahn–Mazurkiewicz for the characterization. Gelbaum–Olmsted treat
space-filling arcs in the plane-sets chapter (unverified citation).

## Object

Classical constructions iterate a self-similar rearrangement of the square (Peano
1890, Hilbert 1891): a uniformly convergent sequence of piecewise-linear curves whose
limit hits every point. A slicker route (reflected in mathlib's proof): map the Cantor
set continuously onto [0,1]² via interleaved binary digits, then extend to [0,1] by
linear interpolation across the removed intervals.

## What it kills

The pre-1890 notion that "curve = 1-dimensional object." Cardinality already showed
|[0,1]| = |[0,1]²| (Cantor), but continuity was believed to forbid it; Peano showed
only *injectivity+continuity* forbids it.

## Debugging uses

- Any proof estimating the "size" of a continuous image by the dimension of the domain
  (Hausdorff dimension, measure, covering numbers) needs Lipschitz or Hölder control:
  a merely continuous image of a null set can have positive area. Lipschitz maps do
  not increase Hausdorff dimension — continuity alone does nothing.
- Space-filling curves are also a *tool*: Hilbert-curve indexing linearizes 2D data
  while roughly preserving locality (databases, load balancing). The counterexample
  and the data structure are the same object; the pathology is the feature.
- Parametrization traps: "parametrize the boundary/region by arc length" assumes
  rectifiability. Space-filling curves have infinite length on every subinterval —
  the extreme case of the Schwarz-lantern lesson that length/area interact badly
  with limits.

## References

Mathlib: `exists_peano_curve` (Counterexamples library). Classical: Peano (1890),
Hilbert (1891); Hahn–Mazurkiewicz for the characterization. Gelbaum–Olmsted treat
space-filling arcs in the plane-sets chapter (unverified citation).

## Object

The certificate witness, as recorded by the triage stage:

Use the 4-cycle x-y-u-v-x. Let E be all four edges, i.e. delta({x,u}). Choose F={xv,yu}, a minimal cut; then G-F has components A={x,y} and B={u,v}. In G[A], HA={xy} is a minimal cut. But in the full graph G, deleting xy leaves the path x-v-u-y, so G-HA is connected. Thus HA is not even a cut in G.

## What it kills

The flawed step of QEDBench problem Algorithms_33, solution 4, reads:

> However, a minimal cut in a subgraph like G[A] or G[B] is also a minimal cut in the entire graph G.

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its
conclusion, refuting the step **as written** (not necessarily the problem's
headline theorem — see the module docstring for scope).

## Why it works

From the Lean module docstring
(`lean/qedbench/ProofCerts/Algorithms/Alg33b.lean`):

**Algorithms_33 (sol4) — a minimal cut of an induced component need not be a cut of G**

The candidate solution asserts:

> A minimal cut in an induced subgraph `G[A]` or `G[B]` (obtained after removing a
> minimal cut `F`) is also a minimal cut in the entire graph `G`.

This is false: an edge set that disconnects the small induced subgraph `G[A]` can be
completely bypassed in `G` by walks that travel through `B`, so it need not even be a
*cut* of `G`, let alone a minimal one.

**Counterexample — the 4-cycle.**
`G` is the cycle `x–y–u–v–x` on vertices `x = 0`, `y = 1`, `u = 2`, `v = 3`, with edges
indexed `xy = 0`, `yu = 1`, `uv = 2`, `vx = 3`.

* `F = {yu, vx}` (edges `1, 3`) is a **minimal edge cut** of `G`: removing it leaves
  only the edges `xy` and `uv`, splitting `G` into the two sides `A = {x, y}` and
  `B = {u, v}`; and dropping either edge of `F` (i.e. removing only one of `yu`, `vx`)
  leaves `G` connected, so no proper nonempty subset of `F` is a cut.
* The induced subgraph `G[A]` on `A = {x, y}` has the single edge `xy`. The set
  `H_A = {xy}` (edge `0`) is a **minimal cut of `G[A]`**: removing `xy` disconnects `x`
  from `y` inside `G[A]`, and `H_A`'s only proper subset `∅` is not a cut (since `G[A]`
  itself is connected).
* But in the **full** graph `G`, deleting `xy` leaves the path `x–v–u–y`, so `G − xy`
  is still connected: `H_A` is **not even a cut of `G`**, hence certainly not a minimal
  cut of `G`. The claim fails.

**Modeling choices.**
* Vertices `= Fin 4`; the four cycle edges are identified with their index `Fin 4` via
  `endpoints`. An edge subset (a candidate cut, i.e. the set of *removed* edges) is a
  membership predicate `S : Fin 4 → Bool`.
* Connectivity of `G − S` is a concrete reachability check: starting from the indicator
  of vertex `0`, apply three rounds of the one-step closure `step` under the surviving
  edges (three rounds suffice on four vertices: the longest induced path, e.g.
  `x–v–u–y` in `G − xy`, has three hops), then test that all of `{0,1,2,3}` is reached.
* The induced subgraph `G[A]` (for `A = {x, y} = {0, 1}`) is modeled by `joinsA`, which
  additionally requires **both endpoints** of a surviving edge to lie in `A`; its
  connectivity check `connectedA` asks only that the `A`-vertices `0` and `1` be
  reached from `x = 0`.
* `IsCut S` (resp. `IsCutA S`) = removing `S` makes `G` (resp. `G[A]`) disconnected.
  Inclusion-minimality is the standard decidable test: a nonempty cut such that erasing
  **any single one of its edges** from the cut destroys the cut property (legitimate
  because "is a cut" is monotone under enlarging the removed-edge set). `IsMinimalCutA`
  also records that the cut consists of `G[A]`-edges. All quantifiers range over the
  finite `Fin 4` of edges/vertices — never over the function type `Fin 4 → Bool` — so
  every `decide` goal stays a finite kernel-robust check (the GT1/Alg33 discipline);
  the final `¬ ∀ S, …` refutation merely *instantiates* the claim at the concrete
  witness `H_A` (the GT20 style), so no enumeration of edge sets is ever needed.

## Debugging uses

- The witness is a minimal, machine-checked regression input for any proof or
  implementation that leans on this step; rebuilding the Lean module re-verifies it.
- The module states the claim faithfully in Mathlib vocabulary; its definitions
  can be reused to audit neighboring steps of the same proof.

## Object

The certificate witness, as recorded by the triage stage:

Use the 3-cube Q3 with unit resistors; take terminals u=000 and v=111. Then graph distance d(u,v)=3 and maximum degree Δ=3, so d/Δ=1. By symmetry, collapsing Hamming-weight levels gives series resistances 1/3, 1/6, 1/3, hence R_eff(u,v)=5/6<1. A finite graph/Laplacian checker can verify this directly.

## What it kills

The flawed step of QEDBench problem Algorithms_8, solution 5, reads:

> The lower bound comes from the fact that the resistance is at least the graph distance (Manhattan distance) divided by the maximum degree

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its
conclusion, refuting the step **as written** (not necessarily the problem's
headline theorem — see the module docstring for scope).

## Why it works

From the Lean module docstring
(`lean/qedbench/ProofCerts/Algorithms/Alg8.lean`):

**Algorithms_8 (sol5) — effective resistance can be BELOW dist/maxdegree (Q3 cube)**

The candidate solution claims:

> "the effective resistance between two vertices is at least the graph distance divided
>  by the maximum degree: `R_eff(u,v) ≥ dist(u,v) / Δ`."

This is false. The correct lower bound is `R_eff(u,v) ≥ 1/Δ` (or `dist/(2m)`-type bounds);
dividing the *whole distance* by `Δ` overshoots, because parallel disjoint paths reduce
resistance below the path length.

**Counterexample — the 3-cube `Q₃` with unit resistors.**
Vertices are the bit-triples `0..7` (`Fin 8`, vertex `i` = binary `i`), edges join pairs at
Hamming distance `1`. Take `u = 000 = 0`, `v = 111 = 7`. Then:

* `Q₃` is `3`-regular, so `Δ = 3`;
* `dist(u,v) = 3`: each edge flips exactly one bit, so `u → v` needs ≥ 3 steps (certified
  below by `Adj u v = false` and "no two-step path"), and `0–1–3–7` is a 3-step path;
  hence `dist/Δ = 3/3 = 1`;
* but `R_eff(u,v) = 5/6 < 1`.

**The harmonic certificate.** By the standard (Kirchhoff/Thomson) characterization,
`R_eff(u,v)` equals the potential gap `φ(u) − φ(v)` of the harmonic potential `φ` carrying
**unit** current from `u` to `v`: with unit resistors, the current on edge `{a,b}` is
`φ(a) − φ(b)`, Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) holds at every internal vertex, and the net
current out of `u` (resp. into `v`) is `1`. On a connected graph this `φ` is unique up to
an additive constant, so the potential gap is well-defined; connectivity of `Q₃` is
certified by the fuel-indexed reachability `reach3`. The explicit solution, by Hamming
level: `φ(000) = 5/6`, `φ = 1/2` on level 1 (`001,010,100`), `φ = 1/3` on level 2
(`011,101,110`), `φ(111) = 0`. Each level-0→1 edge carries `5/6 − 1/2 = 1/3` (3 edges,
total `1`); each 1→2 edge carries `1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6` (6 edges); each 2→3 edge carries
`1/3 − 0 = 1/3` (3 edges). All eight Kirchhoff constraints are verified below, giving
`R_eff = φ(u) − φ(v) = 5/6 − 0 = 5/6 < 1 = dist/Δ`, refuting the claim.

**Modeling choices**
* Vertices are `Fin 8`; the undirected, loop-free adjacency `Adj` is built from the
  explicit 12-edge list of `Q₃`, so every graph fact reduces in the kernel via `decide`
  (the GT1/GT7/GT20 style). `degree` sums `(Adj x ·).toNat` over the eight vertices —
  no `Finset.card` (the GT1 discipline).
* `dist(u,v) = 3` is certified combinatorially: `u ≠ v`, `Adj u v = false`, no middle
  vertex `m` gives a two-step path (`∀ m, (Adj u m && Adj m v) = false`), and the
  explicit path `0–1–3–7` has three edges. Connectivity (used only for the uniqueness
  remark) is the GT20/Alg18-style iterated step function `reach3` — a fuel-indexed
  `Bool` recursion, no `inductive`.
* **Scaled-integer layer (all `decide`).** The potential is stored as the integer table
  `phi6 = 6·φ : Fin 8 → ℤ` (`[5,3,3,2,3,2,2,0]`); the scaled edge current is
  `cur6 a b = if Adj a b then phi6 a − phi6 b else 0` and `net6 a` is its explicit sum
  over the eight vertices. KCL (`net6 = 0` internally), the scaled source/sink strengths
  `net6 u = 6`, `net6 v = −6`, and `phi6 u = 5`, `phi6 v = 0` are all kernel-`decide`d:
  only `Fin 8`/`Bool`/`ℤ` data, never a quantified function type.
* **`ℚ` layer (norm_num).** `phi x = phi6 x / 6 : ℚ`, `current`/`netCurrent` are the
  Ohm-law currents, `Reff = phi u − phi v`. Each `ℚ` fact is *derived* from its scaled
  integer counterpart by `push_cast`/`ring`/`norm_num` — `decide` on `Rat`
  division/coercion is the documented kernel-slow regime (Alg10 discipline), so no
  `Rat` goal ever reaches the kernel's `decide`.

## Debugging uses

- The witness is a minimal, machine-checked regression input for any proof or
  implementation that leans on this step; rebuilding the Lean module re-verifies it.
- The module states the claim faithfully in Mathlib vocabulary; its definitions
  can be reused to audit neighboring steps of the same proof.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Alphabet 2^Xi with Xi = {P1E, P2E, P1C, P2C}. Violating word sigma = {P1E,P2E} . {}^omega with i = 0: sigma,0 |= P1E & P2E and sigma,0 |/= F(P1C|P2C), so sigma,0 |/= (P1E&P2E) -> F(P1C|P2C); hence sigma_hat = sigma[..0] = {P1E,P2E} is exactly the finite prefix the proof declares a bad prefix. Repairing extension: sigma' = {P1E,P2E} . ({P1C})^omega, which has sigma_hat as a prefix and satisfies sigma',0 |= P1E & P2E and sigma',0 |= F(P1C|P2C), therefore sigma',0 |= (P1E&P2E) -> F(P1C|P2C). Claim says: sigma',i |/= (P1E&P2E) -> F(P1C|P2C) for ALL extensions sigma' of sigma_hat; here the implication is SATISFIED at i = 0, so the claim fails on this witness. The same failure occurs for every admissible (sigma_hat, i) pair found: 357/357 admissible pairs (273/273 with i = |sigma_hat|-1) admit a repairing extension inside the searched lasso family; none lacked one.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **In the safety-property argument, the author claims that any extension σ' of the finite prefix σ̂ = σ[..i] still violates the implication at position i, i.e., σ',i ⊭ (P1E ∧ P2E) → F(P1C ∨ P2C), so σ̂ is a bad prefix. This is false: satisfaction of F(P1C ∨ P2C) at position i depends on the infinite suffix beyond the prefix, so an extension can repair the violation.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> for any word $\sigma^\prime\in \left(2^{\Xi} \right)^{\omega}$ such that $\hat\sigma$ is a prefix of $\sigma^\prime$, we have that $\sigma^\prime,i \not \Vdash(P1E \wedge P2E) \rightarrow  (\mathsf{F}\, (P1C \vee P2C))$

Context of the original problem:

> Safety VS. Liveliness Property

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The asserted statement is finitely refutable: it is a universal claim over extensions of a specific finite prefix, so a single finitely-presented (ultimately periodic / lasso) extension satisfying the implication at position i refutes it, and LTL satisfaction on a lasso word is exactly decidable by finite enumeration. For each kept pair it searches all 4624 extensions sigma_hat . u . v^omega with |u| <= 1 and 1 <= |v| <= 2 for one that satisfies the implication at i. Result: all 357 admissible pairs (including all 273 with i = |sigma_hat|-1, the proof's exact configuration) have a repairing extension; 0 had none. The mathematical reason the proof's step is wrong: F(P1C|P2C) evaluated at position i is a property of the infinite suffix from i onward, on which the finite prefix sigma[..i] imposes no constraint beyond the finitely many positions it contains; an extension is free to place a commit (P1C or P2C) at any later position, which makes the eventuality true and the implication hold. ## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Minimal witness (m = 2 bits, n = 2 strings), found by exhaustive enumeration and reproduced by the script.

Setting: LSD radix sort with stable counting-sort passes; bit positions indexed 1..m from most significant (left) to least significant (right); passes run pos = m, m-1, ..., 1, so "later passes" use MORE significant positions k < j.

Input array (in order): ["01", "10"].
Take j = 2 (the last/least-significant position, whose pass the sentence appeals to).

Pass keyed on bit j = 2 (stable): "01" has bit2 = 1, "10" has bit2 = 0, so the array becomes A = ["10", "01"]. The position-j groups are G_0 = {"10"} and G_1 = {"01"}, and in A every member of G_0 precedes every member of G_1.

Later pass, keyed on bit k = 1 (k < j, more significant): "01" has bit1 = 0, "10" has bit1 = 1, so the stable pass yields B = ["01", "10"].

Formal violation of the quoted sentence: a permutation that "only reorders strings within the groups that share the same bit at position j" can never change the relative order of two strings lying in different groups. Here u = "10" (bit_j = 0) and v = "01" (bit_j = 1) lie in different position-j groups, and
  index_A(u) = 0 < index_A(v) = 1  (u before v),
  index_B(u) = 1 > index_B(v) = 0  (u after v).
Claim says index_B(u) < index_B(v); here index_B(u) = 1 > index_B(v) = 0. The later pass moved a string from one position-j group ahead of a string from the other group, i.e. it interleaved the groups rather than reordering within them.

This is not an isolated accident: the exhaustive scan found the violation in 1,100,924 of the 1,157,264 arrays searched (e.g. 2 of the 16 arrays already at m = n = 2).

Secondary exhaustive check over the same 1,157,264 arrays: the proof's CONCLUSION (if s_i = t_i for all i < j, s_j = 0, t_j = 1, then s never ends up after t in the final array) has NO counterexample. So the theorem stands; it is exactly the quoted justification that is false, and it is false for the reason stated in the target claim — the correct argument needs the unused hypothesis s_i = t_i for all i < j (which makes s and t have equal keys in every later pass, so plain stability preserves their order), not any "later passes only permute within position-j groups" property.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The proof's stated justification for the crucial stability step: that the passes after iteration k=j "only reorder strings within the groups that share the same bit at position j". This universal claim about later stable counting-sort passes is false; a stable sort by a more significant bit k<j freely interleaves strings drawn from the two position-j groups. The proof's conclusion (s cannot move ahead of t) actually requires the unused hypothesis s_i = t_i for all i<j, which this sentence never invokes.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> those later sorts are *stable* and only reorder strings **within** the groups that share the same bit at position j

Context of the original problem:

> Problem Statement
> Problem: Algorithms - 30
> Consider a collection of n binary strings, where each string has length m. The lexico-
> graphical order is defined as follows: for strings s and t, we define s < t if there is a
> position j ∈{1, . . . , m} such that sj < tj and si = ti for all indices 1 ≤i < j. Prove
> the existence of an algorithm that sorts these n strings according to this lexicographical
> order with a total running time of O(nm).
> 1

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The sentence asserts a universal property of every later stable counting-sort pass: that such a pass only reorders strings within the blocks determined by the bit at position j. A permutation that acts only within blocks is exactly one that preserves the relative order of any two elements in different blocks, so the assertion is a finitely-quantified statement over finite arrays of finite binary strings and is refuted by a single array + j + k + pair whose relative order flips. The script enumerates every array in ({0,1}^m)^n for m in {2,3,4,5}, n in {2,3,4} (1,157,264 arrays, repetitions allowed, entries tracked by identity index so duplicates are handled), runs the full LSD radix sort, snapshots the array after each pass, and tests the block-order-preservation condition for every j, every later key position k < j, and every pair of entries. All computation is exact and combinatorial (ints, tuples of 0/1 bits, index comparisons); no floats, no randomness, deterministic itertools.product enumeration. A violation was found immediately at m = n = 2 with input ["01","10"], j = 2, k = 1, and in 95.1% of all arrays searched. A second exhaustive pass over the same space confirmed zero violations of the statement the proof was actually trying to prove, isolating the defect to the justification (which never invokes the hypothesis s_i = t_i for i < j) rather than to the theorem.
